standard.title: Develop historical questions
standard.description: develop historical questions about the past to inform historical inquiry
standard.prior_knowledge: Students develop questions about objects, people, places and events in the past and present (AC9HH7S01). They can formulate basic historical questions. They have not yet developed multi-level question hierarchies (key question plus related sub-questions), questions about historical significance with measurable criteria, or the capacity to review and revise questions when inquiry produces unexpected findings.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop historical questions about the past that inform historical inquiry — including a key question, related sub-questions about evidence and theories, questions about historical significance with measurable criteria, and the capacity to review questions when unexpected findings emerge.

nodes.label: Key inquiry question
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop a key historical question that focuses an inquiry — framed to invite explanation rather than description, grounded in a specific historical context.
nodes.minimum_width: One key historical question framed to invite explanation (why/how) about a specific historical context.
nodes.typical_width: A key question that focuses the inquiry and is appropriately scoped — not too broad (e.g. 'What happened in the Middle Ages?') and not too narrow (e.g. 'What year did Rome fall?'). Examples: 'How did the decline of Rome's western empire change the organisation of European society?' or 'Why did Easter Island (Rapa Nui) society decline?'
wider: Develop multiple candidate key questions for the same inquiry and evaluate which is best scoped — identifying what each question foregrounds and what it leaves out
Examine how different key questions about the same event (e.g. the Black Death) would direct inquiry in different directions — towards causes, effects, experiences or significance
nodes.hinge_reason: A poorly framed key question either produces description rather than explanation or is unanswerably broad. Students who cannot frame an inquiry-focused question cannot generate sub-questions, assess significance or review their inquiry purposefully.

response_modes.reason: Students need explicit practice distinguishing inquiry questions (which invite explanation and require research) from factual questions (which have known answers) and opinion questions (which require no evidence). Scaffold the criteria: does this question require historical investigation to answer?

success_criteria: Develops a key historical question framed to invite explanation (using why or how) about a specific historical context
The question is appropriately scoped — neither too broad nor too narrow — to focus a historical inquiry

nodes.label: Sub-questions and significance questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop related sub-questions to support the key inquiry — including questions about evidence, theories, and historical significance with measurable criteria.
nodes.minimum_width: At least two sub-questions that support the key inquiry question, including at least one about evidence and one about significance.
nodes.typical_width: A hierarchy of questions: key question + related sub-questions about evidence ('What evidence is there?', 'What theories have been developed?') + questions about significance with measurable criteria ('How many people were affected by the Black Death?', 'How long did it last?', 'How deeply did it change society?').
wider: Develop questions about historical significance that explicitly reference the criteria of significance — scale, duration, depth of change, legacy — rather than just asking 'How significant was this?'
Examine how sub-questions can be organised into a logical inquiry sequence — moving from factual grounding to interpretive analysis to significance judgement

response_modes.reason: Developing well-structured question hierarchies is a skill that requires practice. Students need multiple opportunities to build key question + sub-questions sets before they can do this reliably and independently.

success_criteria: Develops at least two sub-questions that relate to and support the key inquiry question
Includes at least one question about evidence and one about historical significance with measurable criteria

nodes.label: Reviewing and revising questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can review and revise their inquiry questions when unexpected or challenging findings emerge during investigation.
nodes.minimum_width: At least one example of how an inquiry question was revised or refined in response to what was found during investigation.
nodes.typical_width: The capacity to identify when a question needs revision — when evidence doesn't support the framing, when the scope is wrong, or when the inquiry reveals a more interesting question. Example: reviewing 'How was the organisation of Japanese society influenced by world events?' when research reveals the complexity of Japan's isolation policy under the Tokugawa.
wider: Practice reviewing questions at multiple points in an inquiry — identifying what the initial question assumed, what investigation revealed, and how the question should be revised to reflect a more accurate historical understanding
Examine how historians revise research questions as new evidence emerges — using the example of how Polynesian expansion theories have changed as archaeological evidence has grown

response_modes.reason: Question revision integrates the capacity to frame questions (Node 1) with the capacity to assess whether the question is working in practice (Node 2 + emerging research). Invest in helping students see inquiry as iterative, not linear.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one point in an inquiry where a question needed revision and explains why
Develops a revised question that better reflects the findings of the investigation
